massospondylus:enwiki:5.title: Massospondylus (Previously recognised species from southern Africa)

massospondylus:enwiki:13.title: Massospondylus (Posture, range of motion, and function of thumb claw)

facts.statement: The genus Massospondylus was described by Richard Owen in 1854.
facts.quote: authority: Owen, 1854

facts.statement: Massospondylus lived during the Hettangian, Sinemurian, and Pliensbachian ages.
facts.quote: The genus lived during the Hettangian, Sinemurian, and Pliensbachian ages

facts.statement: Most Massospondylus fossils are found in the upper Elliot and Clarens formations of South Africa and Lesotho.
facts.quote: Most fossils come from the upper Elliot and Clarens formations of South Africa and Lesotho

facts.statement: Massospondylus fossils are also found in the Forest Sandstone and Mpandi Formation of Zimbabwe.
facts.quote: but the genus is also found in the Forest Sandstone and the Mpandi Formation of Zimbabwe

facts.statement: Massospondylus is one of the first dinosaurs to be named, described by Richard Owen in 1854 from South African remains.
facts.quote: It was described by Richard Owen in 1854 from remains discovered in South Africa, and is thus one of the first dinosaurs to have been named

facts.statement: The name Massospondylus means 'longer vertebra'.
facts.quote: The name Massospondylus means longer vertebra

facts.statement: Massospondylus was 4 to 6 meters long with a long neck and tail, small head, and slender body.
facts.quote: The genus was 4 - 6 m long, with a long neck and tail, a small head, and a slender body

facts.statement: Massospondylus is now considered to have been bipedal, despite earlier depictions as quadrupedal.
facts.quote: Although Massospondylus was long depicted as quadrupedal (four-legged), it is now considered to have been bipedal (two-legged)

facts.statement: Massospondylus was probably a herbivore.
facts.quote: This dinosaur was probably a herbivore (plant-eater)

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a sharp thumb claw on each hand, likely used for feeding by uprooting vegetation or pulling down branches.
facts.quote: On each of its hands, it bore a sharp thumb claw that was probably used in feeding, possibly to uproot vegetation or to pull down branches while rearing up

facts.statement: Fossils of Massospondylus include clutches of eggs with embryos, representing some of the oldest amniote eggs and embryos known.
facts.quote: Clutches of eggs have been found, some of which contained embryos; these are among the oldest eggs and embryos of an amniote in the fossil record

facts.statement: Massospondylus eggshells were extremely thin, measuring less than 0.1 mm.
facts.quote: The eggshell was extremely thin, less than 0.1 mm, unlike the much thicker eggshells in later dinosaurs

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Massospondylus embryos were quadrupedal with proportionally longer arms and large heads, shifting to bipedalism later in growth.
facts.quote: The embryos had proportionally longer arms than adults and a very large head, leading researchers to suggest that they were quadrupedal and shifted to a bipedal posture later during growth

facts.statement: Newer research suggests Massospondylus was bipedal at all ages.
facts.quote: Newer research instead suggested that Massospondylus was bipedal at all ages

facts.statement: The oldest known Massospondylus specimen was approximately 20 years old.
facts.quote: The oldest known specimen was around 20 years of age

facts.statement: Massospondylus is often classified within the family Massospondylidae.
facts.quote: Within sauropodomorphs, Massospondylus is often classified in the family Massospondylidae

facts.statement: The first fossils of Massospondylus were described by Richard Owen in 1854.
facts.quote: The first fossils of Massospondylus were described by Richard Owen in 1854

facts.statement: The name Massospondylus is derived from the Greek words for 'longer' and 'vertebra'.
facts.quote: The name Massospondylus (meaning longer vertebra) is derived from the Greek μάσσων (massōn) longer and σπόνδυλος (spondylos) vertebra

facts.statement: The original fossils were likely found disarticulated, making it difficult to determine if they belonged to the same species.
facts.quote: All these bones were probably found disarticulated (not connected to each other), making it difficult to determine whether or not they belonged to the same species

facts.statement: The entire Orpen collection, including the type material for Massospondylus, was lost during World War II bombings, leaving only illustrations and plaster casts.
facts.quote: Many specimens that have been pivotal in the history of science were lost, as well as the entire Orpen collection, including Massospondylus, Pachyspondylus, and Leptospondylus, of which only illustrations and plaster casts remain

facts.statement: It is debated whether basal sauropodomorphs like Massospondylus may have been omnivorous.
facts.quote: although some have speculated that basal sauropodomorphs may have been omnivorous

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding whether Massospondylus was bipedal only as an adult or bipedal at all ages.
facts.quote: Newer research instead suggested that Massospondylus was bipedal at all ages

facts.statement: A British-South African expedition discovered a Massospondylus hatchling skeleton in Lesotho in 1961, initially misidentifying it as the varanopid Heleosaurus.
facts.quote: Already in 1961, a British-South African palaeontological expedition discovered the skeleton of a hatchling (SAM-PK-K413) at Mafeteng, Lesotho, although this specimen was first misidentified as the varanopid Heleosaurus.

facts.statement: Michael Cooper published a comprehensive study of Zimbabwean Massospondylus in 1981, describing the skeleton except for the skull, which was not available at the time.
facts.quote: In 1981, Michael Cooper published a comprehensive monograph on the Zimbabwean Massospondylus material, describing the entire skeleton apart from the skull, of which no material was available.

facts.statement: Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues provided a comprehensive description of Massospondylus skulls in 2004 and proposed the first formal diagnosis for M. carinatus.
facts.quote: In 2004, Hans-Dieter Sues and colleagues provided a more comprehensive description of the same four skulls, and proposed the first diagnosis of M. carinatus (the set of distinguishing features).

facts.statement: Yates and Barrett proposed in 2010 to designate specimen BP/1/4934 as the neotype for Massospondylus because the original syntype series lacked distinguishing features.
facts.quote: Consequently, Yates and Barrett proposed in 2010 to designate a different specimen, BP/1/4934, as the neotype specimen (the new representative specimen).

facts.statement: The neotype specimen of Massospondylus, nicknamed "Big Momma," was found in March 1980 on a farm near Clocolan, South Africa, by Lucas Huma and James Kitching.
facts.quote: The specimen, nicknamed "Big Momma" although its sex is unknown, was found in March 1980 on a farm near Clocolan, South Africa, by Lucas Huma and James Kitching.

facts.statement: As of 2019, the "Big Momma" specimen is the largest and most complete Massospondylus and likely the most complete basal sauropodomorph found in Africa.
facts.quote: As of 2019, it is the largest and most complete Massospondylus specimen and probably the most complete basal (early diverging) sauropodomorph specimen discovered in Africa.

facts.statement: The skull of the "Big Momma" neotype was described in detail in 2018, and the rest of the skeleton was described in 2019.
facts.quote: The skull was described in detail in 2018 by Chapelle and Jonah Choiniere, while Barrett and colleagues described the remainder of the skeleton in 2019.

facts.statement: The "Big Momma" specimen is divided into seven blocks, with the heaviest weighing approximately 35 kg.
facts.quote: However, the specimen has been divided into seven individual blocks, the heaviest of which is about 35 kg in weight.

facts.statement: The "Big Momma" specimen underwent extensive restoration in the 2000s because repeated handling caused the fossils to deteriorate.
facts.quote: In the 2000s, the specimen was extensively restored after it became apparent that the fossils were deteriorating due to repeated handling.

facts.statement: Currently, two species of Massospondylus are recognized: M. carinatus and M. kaalae.
facts.quote: Besides the type species Massospondylus carinatus, one additional species, Massospondylus kaalae, is currently recognised.

facts.statement: Barrett identified the skull as a new species in 2004 and formally named it M. kaalae in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2004, Barrett noted that this skull belonged to a new species, which he named M. kaalae in 2009.

facts.statement: The species M. kaalae is named in honor of Sheena Kaal, the museum's collections manager for Karoo vertebrate fossils.
facts.quote: The species is named in honor of the museum's collections manager for the Karoo vertebrate fossils, Sheena Kaal, for her assistance to numerous scientists who have studied specimens at the museum.

facts.statement: Seeley tentatively named the species M. browni in 1895, though its assignment to Massospondylus was uncertain.
facts.quote: In 1895, Seeley named the species M. browni, although its assignment to Massospondylus was only tentative.

facts.statement: M. browni was based on vertebrae and limb bones discovered north of the Witteberg by Alfred Brown.
facts.quote: This species was based on two neck, two back, and three tail vertebrae as well as femora and toe bones that were discovered north of the Witteberg by Alfred Brown.

facts.statement: In 1906, von Huene concluded that the material originally assigned to M. browni belonged to two separate species.
facts.quote: In 1906, von Huene concluded that the vertebrae and femora of M. browni belonged to two separate species.

facts.statement: A partial skeleton assigned to M. browni in 1920 was later moved to M. harriesi and is now considered part of M. carinatus.
facts.quote: In 1920, Egbert Cornelis Nicolaas van Hoepen assigned a partial skeleton to M. browni, which was later assigned to M. harriesi and is now listed as a specimen of M. carinatus.

facts.statement: A 2004 review classified M. browni as an indeterminate sauropodomorph.
facts.quote: M. browni was considered an indeterminate sauropodomorph in a 2004 review by Peter Galton and Paul Upchurch.

facts.statement: Robert Broom named M. harriesi in 1911 based on forelimb and hind limb parts found near Fouriesburg.
facts.quote: M. harriesi was named by Robert Broom in 1911 based on parts of a forelimb and hind limb discovered near Fouriesburg.

facts.statement: M. harriesi and M. schwarzi were considered indeterminate sauropodomorphs in a 2004 review.
facts.quote: Both species were considered as indeterminate sauropodomorphs in the 2004 review.

facts.statement: Several South African species originally assigned to different genera were later considered synonyms of Massospondylus but are now regarded as indeterminate.
facts.quote: Several other species from South Africa have originally been assigned to different genera, were later regarded as synonyms of Massospondylus, and are currently regarded as indeterminate (too incomplete to be classified).

facts.statement: Seeley named Hortalotarsus skirtopodus in 1894 based on a specimen from the Clarens Formation near Barkly East.
facts.quote: Hortalotarsus skirtopodus was named by Seeley in 1894, based on a specimen found in the Clarens Formation near Barkly East.

facts.statement: Most of the original Hortalotarsus skirtopodus skeleton was destroyed during preparation, leaving only a fragmentary hind limb.
facts.quote: Most of the original skeleton was destroyed in an attempt to remove it from the rock matrix, and only a fragmentary hind limb remains.

facts.statement: Broom named Aetonyx palustris, Gryponyx africanus, and Gyposaurus capensis in 1911.
facts.quote: Aetonyx palustris, Gryponyx africanus and Gyposaurus capensis were all named by Broom in 1911.

facts.statement: Broom named Gryponyx transvaalensis in 1912 based on two foot bones found in the Bushveld Sandstone Formation in Limpopo Province.
facts.quote: One year later, in 1912, Broom named Gryponyx transvaalensis from two foot bones (an ungual and a metatarsal) discovered in the Bushveld Sandstone Formation in Limpopo Province.

facts.statement: Haughton named Thecodontosaurus minor in 1918 based on a neck vertebra, tibia, and ilium from the Elliot Formation near Maclear.
facts.quote: Thecodontosaurus minor was named by Haughton in 1918 based on a neck vertebra, a tibia, and an ilium found in the Elliot Formation near Maclear.

facts.statement: Haughton named Thecodontosaurus dubius and Gryponyx taylori in 1924.
facts.quote: In 1924, Haughton erected another species of Thecodontosaurus, T. dubius, as well as Gryponyx taylori.

facts.statement: Galton and Cluver assigned several species to M. harriesi in 1976.
facts.quote: In 1976, Galton and Cluver assigned Aetonyx palustris, Gryponyx africanus, Gryponyx taylori, Dromicosaurus gracilis, and Thecodontosaurus dubius to M. harriesi.

facts.statement: Cooper considered all related taxa as synonyms of M. carinatus in 1981.
facts.quote: Cooper, in 1981, instead considered all taxa as synonyms of M. carinatus.

facts.statement: Galton listed some species as synonyms of M. carinatus in 1990, but a 2004 review considered all as indeterminate sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: Galton, in a 1990 review, only listed Aetonyx palustris, Gryponyx africanus, Gyposaurus capensis, and Gryponyx taylori as synonyms of M. carinatus, while the 2004 review considers all species to be indeterminate sauropodomorphs rather than synonyms of Massospondylus.

facts.statement: R. Lydekker described two species of Massospondylus from Indian fossils in 1890.
facts.quote: In 1890, Lydekker described the species M. hislopi and M. rawesi from fossils found in India.

facts.statement: The species M. rawesi was originally defined by a single tooth discovered in the Takli Formation.
facts.quote: M. rawesi was based on a single tooth found by Mr. Rawes in the Upper Cretaceous Takli Formation in Maharashtra.

facts.statement: Fossils from the US described in 1985 were reclassified into the new genus Sarahsaurus in 2010–2011.
facts.quote: The material from the US, which consists of a nearly complete skull with skeleton described in 1985, was assigned to the new and closely related genus Sarahsaurus in 2010–2011.

facts.statement: Argentinian fossils described in 1999 were identified as a new genus, Adeopapposaurus, in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, the Argentinian material, which consists of several partial skeletons described in 1999, has likewise been recognised as a new genus, Adeopapposaurus.

facts.statement: The discovery of new genera in the 21st century has led to debates about the validity of earlier Massospondylus identifications.
facts.quote: During the 21st century, two additional massospondylid genera were identified in southern Africa, raising the question of whether all of the previous identifications of Massospondylus specimens were correct.

facts.statement: Massospondylus is classified as a mid-sized sauropodomorph dinosaur.
facts.quote: Massospondylus was a mid-sized sauropodomorph.

facts.statement: A 2019 study estimated the largest known specimen of Massospondylus to be approximately 5 meters long.
facts.quote: In 2019, Barrett and colleagues estimated the particularly large neotype specimen at around 5 m in length.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the length of Massospondylus to be 4.3 meters in a 2024 publication.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul, in a popular book published in 2024, estimated Massospondylus to be 4.3 m in length.

facts.statement: Frank Seebacher estimated the body weight of Massospondylus at 136.7 kg in 2001.
facts.quote: The body weight was estimated at 136.7 kg by Frank Seebacher in 2001, assuming a body length of 4 m.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the body weight of Massospondylus to be 195 kg.
facts.quote: Paul instead gave a body weight of 195 kg.

facts.statement: Massospondylus possessed a slender body, long neck, and proportionally small head typical of basal sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: It was a typical basal sauropodomorph, with a slender body, a long neck, and a proportionally very small head.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a more slender build than the similar but larger dinosaur Plateosaurus.
facts.quote: It had a slighter build than Plateosaurus, an otherwise similar but larger dinosaur.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that basal sauropodomorphs likely possessed air sacs and a bird-like flow-through lung system.
facts.quote: Basal sauropodomorphs probably had air sacs and possibly a bird-like flow-through lung.

facts.statement: Unlike some relatives like Plateosaurus, the vertebrae of Massospondylus lack signs of pneumaticity.
facts.quote: Although some basal sauropodomorphs such as Plateosaurus show incipient pneumaticity in their vertebrae, those of Massospondylus are apneumatic (lack any signs of pneumaticity).

facts.statement: The skull of Massospondylus was small, measuring about half the length of the femur.
facts.quote: The skull of Massospondylus was small and approximately half the length of the femur (thigh bone).

facts.statement: The external nostril of Massospondylus was roughly half the size of its eye socket.
facts.quote: At the front of the skull was the large external naris (nostril), which was roughly half the size of the orbit (eye socket).

facts.statement: A unique feature of the Massospondylus skull is that its basipterygoid processes form an angle of approximately 35 degrees, unlike other basal sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: A single distinguishing feature is found in the skull: the basipterygoid processes, a pair of bony extensions that braces the braincase against the palate, form an angle of ca. 35°, whereas this angle is much larger in all other basal sauropodomorphs in which it can be measured.

facts.statement: The front bone of the upper jaw in Massospondylus consistently held four teeth on each side.
facts.quote: The premaxilla, the front bone of the upper jaw, showed the constant number of four teeth per side in all known skulls.

facts.statement: The number of teeth in the upper jaw bone of Massospondylus varied between 14 and 22.
facts.quote: In the maxilla, the tooth count varied from 14 to 22.

facts.statement: The upper teeth of Massospondylus had serrated edges with between three and eight serrations per side.
facts.quote: The upper halves of the tooth crowns had serrated edges, with three to eight serrations on each side.

facts.statement: Massospondylus replaced its teeth throughout life, creating a saw-like profile where neighboring teeth were of different heights.
facts.quote: The teeth were replaced throughout life, as in other dinosaurs. This resulted in neighbouring teeth being of different heights, giving the tooth row a profile similar to a saw.

facts.statement: A 2013 study estimated that individual teeth in Massospondylus were used for only 17 to 30 days before replacement.
facts.quote: a 2013 study estimated that a tooth remained in use for only 17 to 30 days.

facts.statement: Front teeth in Massospondylus had pointed, curved tips, while rear teeth were broad, flat, and symmetrical.
facts.quote: Teeth closer to the front of the snout had pointed tips and were slightly curved, unlike the posterior teeth that were spatulate (with a broad, flat tip) and more symmetrical.

facts.statement: The teeth of Massospondylus were proportionally longer and slimmer than those of Plateosaurus.
facts.quote: The teeth were proportionally longer and slenderer than those of Plateosaurus.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a vertebral column consisting of nine neck vertebrae, thirteen back vertebrae, three hip vertebrae, and at least forty tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The vertebral column was composed of nine cervical (neck) vertebrae, 13 dorsal (back) vertebrae, three sacral (hip) vertebrae, and at least 40 tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: The front neck vertebrae of Massospondylus had elongated neural spines with a hook-like protuberance at the front end, distinguishing it from other species.
facts.quote: In the anterior cervicals, the neural spine (the bony keel that formed the top of each vertebra) was elongated, and its anterior end had a hook-like protuberance that constitutes another distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a shoulder blade with a symmetrical upper expansion, unlike related genera where the front expansion was much larger than the rear.
facts.quote: The shoulder blade had an expanded upper end. This expansion was more symmetrical than in related genera, in which the dorsal (front) expansion was much larger than the ventral (rear) expansion, and is a distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had forelimbs half the length of its hind limbs but powerful enough to support large arm muscles attached to a broad deltopectoral crest on the humerus.
facts.quote: The forelimbs were only half the length of the hind limbs but quite powerful, as indicated by a broad flange on the upper portion of the humerus called the deltopectoral crest, which provided attachment areas for a large arm musculature.

facts.statement: The deltopectoral crest on Massospondylus extended for approximately 60% of the humerus length, which is longer than in related genera.
facts.quote: This crest was longer than in related genera, extending for ca. 60% of the length of the bone, which is a distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a proportionally short lower arm with an ulna measuring around 60% of the humerus length.
facts.quote: The lower arm was proportionally short, with the ulna measuring around 60% of the length of the humerus, which is another distinguishing feature.

facts.statement: The phalangeal formula of the Massospondylus hand was 2-3-4-3-2, indicating the number of finger bones from thumb to fifth digit.
facts.quote: The phalangeal formula of the hand, which states the number of finger bones from the thumb to the fifth digit, was 2-3-4-3-2.

facts.statement: Massospondylus had a large, curved claw on the first toe that was flattened from side to side.
facts.quote: The foot also had a large claw on the first digit, which was curved and flattened laterally (side-to-side).

facts.statement: The claws on the middle three toes of Massospondylus were smaller, less curved, and flattened from top to bottom.
facts.quote: The claws on the middle three digits instead were smaller, less curved, and flattened dorsoventrally (top to bottom).

facts.statement: The fifth toe of Massospondylus consisted of only a single bone and lacked a claw.
facts.quote: The fifth toe only had a single toe bone and no claw.

facts.statement: The phalangeal formula of the Massospondylus foot was 2-3-4-5-1.
facts.quote: The phalangeal formula of the foot was 2-3-4-5-1.

facts.statement: In 1888, Lydekker classified Massospondylus as a dinosaur within the family Anchisauridae and the group Theropoda.
facts.quote: In 1888, Lydekker demonstrated that Massospondylus is a genus of dinosaur, and classified it in the family Anchisauridae, within Theropoda.

facts.statement: In 1920, von Huene created the group Prosauropoda to unite early long-necked dinosaurs including Massospondylus.
facts.quote: In 1920, von Huene named the new group Prosauropoda to unite the early long-necked dinosaurs including Massospondylus.

facts.statement: In 1932, von Huene named the group Sauropodomorpha containing Prosauropoda and Sauropoda, moving Massospondylus out of Theropoda.
facts.quote: In 1932, he also named the new group Sauropodomorpha, which contained his Prosauropoda as well as Sauropoda, abandoning the traditional classification of Massospondylus and related genera within Theropoda.

facts.statement: In the 1990 edition of The Dinosauria, Galton resurrected the family Massospondylidae containing Massospondylus as its sole member.
facts.quote: In the 1990 edition of the encyclopedia The Dinosauria, Galton recognised additional prosauropod families including a resurrected Massospondylidae that contained Massospondylus as its only member.

facts.statement: The family Massospondylidae has been recognized by the majority of studies since its resurrection.
facts.quote: Massospondylidae has since been recognised by a majority of studies.

facts.statement: The family Massospondylidae typically includes Adeopapposaurus, Coloradisaurus, Leyesaurus, and Lufengosaurus in addition to Massospondylus.
facts.quote: Besides Massospondylus itself, Massospondylidae typically includes Adeopapposaurus, Coloradisaurus, Leyesaurus, and Lufengosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2007, Adam Yates named the group Massopoda as a subgroup of Plateosauria including Massospondylidae and sauropods but excluding Plateosauridae.
facts.quote: Adam Yates, in 2007, named the group Massopoda as a sub-group of Plateosauria that includes Massospondylidae and sauropods but not Plateosauridae.

facts.statement: Massospondylus likely had a herbivorous or omnivorous diet.
facts.quote: Basal sauropodomorphs such as Massospondylus may have been herbivorous or omnivorous.

facts.statement: A 2004 study by Galton and Upchurch found that Massospondylus cranial features resemble those of herbivorous reptiles more than carnivorous ones.
facts.quote: In 2004, Galton and Upchurch found that cranial characteristics (such as jaw articulation) of most basal sauropodomorphs are closer to those of herbivorous reptiles than those of carnivorous ones

facts.statement: In 2000, Barrett proposed that Massospondylus supplemented its plant diet with small prey or carrion.
facts.quote: In 2000, Barrett proposed that basal sauropodomorphs supplemented their herbivorous diets with small prey or carrion.

facts.statement: In 1986, Crompton and Attridge suggested Massospondylus had a weak bite due to its light skull construction and long tooth rows.
facts.quote: In their 1986 study, Alfred Crompton and John Attridge suggested that Massospondylus and Plateosaurus had weak bites because their skulls were lightly constructed and had long tooth rows.

facts.statement: In one specimen, the preserved gastroliths made up approximately 1% of the body mass.
facts.quote: In one of these specimens, the preserved gastroliths made up ca. 1% of the body mass.

facts.statement: In 2007, Wings and Sander argued that the gastroliths in Massospondylus were likely not used as an effective gastric mill.
facts.quote: However, Oliver Wings and Martin Sander showed in 2007 that the polished nature and the abundance of those stones precluded their use as an effective gastric mill in most non-theropod dinosaurs, including Massospondylus.

facts.statement: In 1986, Crompton and Attridge suggested Massospondylus had a horny beak on its lower jaw to compensate for overbite length differences.
facts.quote: In 1986, Crompton and Attridge described skulls of Massospondylus as possessing pronounced overbites and suggested the presence of a horny beak on the tip of the lower jaw to make up the difference in length.

facts.statement: Recent studies consider the presence of a beak in Massospondylus unlikely, suggesting earlier observations of overbites were misinterpretations of crushed skulls.
facts.quote: However, the difference in length may be a misinterpretation and caused by crushing of the skull in a top–bottom plane, and more recent studies consider the possession of a beak as unlikely.

facts.statement: In 2007, Barrett and Upchurch contradicted Cooper's view, noting that only the hindmost neck vertebrae were inclined, allowing sufficient horizontal neck movement.
facts.quote: This was contradicted by Barrett and Upchurch in 2007, who noted that only the hindmost cervicals showed inclined zygapophyses, allowing sufficient horizontal movement of the neck as a whole.

facts.statement: In 2007, Bonnan and Senter argued that Massospondylus was restricted to bipedal gaits rather than being quadrupedal.
facts.quote: Although long assumed to have been quadrupedal (four-legged), Matthew Bonnan and Phil Senter questioned this in 2007, arguing that the animal was restricted to bipedal (two-legged) gaits.

facts.statement: The ossification of the thumb in Massospondylus embryos before other limbs suggests it had important functions at early developmental stages.
facts.quote: In the embryo, the thumb was already ossified while most other parts of the hands and feet were unossified, which might suggest that it had important functions already at early developmental stages.

facts.statement: Specimen BP-1-5241 shows Massospondylus had well-developed clavicles joined in a furcula-like arrangement that prevented shoulder blade rotation.
facts.quote: However, the Massospondylus specimen BP-1-5241 preserves well-developed clavicles that are joined in a furcula-like arrangement, showing that they acted as a clasp between the right and left shoulder blades, prohibiting any rotation of these bones.

facts.statement: In 1993, Chinsamy-Turan found that Massospondylus growth was cyclic, forming one growth ring per year based on femur analysis.
facts.quote: The first such study for Massospondylus was conducted in 1993 by Anusuya Chinsamy-Turan who, based on femora of different sizes, found that growth was cyclic, with one growth ring formed each year.

facts.statement: Chinsamy-Turan suggested Massospondylus had indeterminate growth because no external fundamental system was found in its bones.
facts.quote: Because an external fundamental system (tightly packed growth rings that indicate that growth had stopped) was absent, she suggested that Massospondylus had indeterminate growth (growth throughout life).

facts.statement: In 2022, Chapelle and colleagues found substantial growth variation in 27 Massospondylus specimens, suggesting developmental plasticity was widespread in basal sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: In 2022, Chapelle and colleagues analysed multiple different bones from 27 Massospondylus specimens and instead found substantial growth variation as in Plateosaurus, suggesting that developmental plasticity was widespread in basal sauropodomorphs.

facts.statement: Chapelle and colleagues argue Massospondylus had determinate growth, contradicting Chinsamy's 1993 finding of indeterminate growth.
facts.quote: These authors also argue that Massospondylus had determinate growth, contradicting the 1993 study of Chinsamy that suggested that growth was indeterminate.

facts.statement: The oldest analyzed Massospondylus specimen had stopped growing at an estimated age of 20 years.
facts.quote: Growth had stopped in the oldest analysed specimen, which was estimated at 20 years old.

facts.statement: Excavations between 2005 and 2012 revealed ten egg clutches containing up to 34 eggs each at the Rooidraai nesting site.
facts.quote: After additional excavations at the site between 2005 and 2012, Reisz and colleagues reported that 10 egg clutches from at least four fossiliferous horizons had been found, with up to 34 eggs per clutch

facts.statement: Massospondylus eggs are among the oldest known amniote eggs in the fossil record, found alongside those of Lufengosaurus and Mussaurus.
facts.quote: Massospondylus eggs are amongst the oldest known amniote eggs from the fossil record, together with the roughly contemporaneous eggs of Lufengosaurus and Mussaurus

facts.statement: The eggshell had a thick membrane covered by a calcite layer less than 0.1 mm thick with a rugged surface and few unevenly distributed pores.
facts.quote: The eggshell consisted of a thick membrane covered by a layer of calcite that was very thin, less than 0.1 mm, and had a rugged surface with few, unevenly distributed pores

facts.statement: The most complete embryonic skeleton found is articulated and measures about 8.1 cm in snout-vent length.
facts.quote: The most complete embryonic skeleton is still articulated and belonged to an individual measuring about 8.1 cm in snout-vent length

facts.statement: Embryos had large heads with short snouts and orbits measuring 39% of the total skull length.
